To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
– For the programs we examined, the average application speedup is about 2.0, with a standard deviation of 1.0, so there is significant variation.
– For the applications we have studied, the rate of reallocation should be between 10% and 50% per second.
– Speedup varies significantly from job to job.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of scheduling policies for parallel machines, and in particular with policies for multiprocessor systems.
the design of scheduling policies for shared-memory multiprocessors.
the design of scheduling policies for multiprocessor environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have not yet reached a definitive answer on the best way to schedule multiprocessors.
there is no single answer to the questions of what is the appropriate rate of reallocation and whether or not speedup information can be measured at runtime. Rather
there is no conclusive statement to be made. We do not claim to have identified a single “right” policy, or even a single “right way”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for multiprocessor scheduling, the design of appropriate policies must consider both abstract properties of the workload and concrete properties of the applications.
the most appropriate scheduling policy is a hybrid of static and dynamic allocation.
there is a significant potential for multiprocessor scheduling policies to provide improved performance, but that the choice of an appropriate policy is not straightforward.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the behavior of real parallel applications on a shared-memory multiprocessors is sufficiently varied that there can be no “one size fits all” scheduling policy.
the choice of a scheduling policy is highly application-dependent, and that it may be difficult to design a single policy that is appropriate across all applications.
there is a wide variation among applications in the characteristics of interest to scheduling policy designers.
